Page 4

Warm Up — Uncoupled IVP

Consider the initial value problem:

\[\vec{r}\,'(t) = \begin{bmatrix} x' \\ y' \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 5x \\ -5y \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \vec{r}(0) = \begin{bmatrix} -4 \\ -1 \end{bmatrix}\]

The parametric equation of the solution curve is \(\vec{r}(t) = \begin{bmatrix} x(t) \\ y(t) \end{bmatrix}\) where the student is asked to find:

\[x(t) = \quad \boxed{\phantom{-4e^{5t}}}\] \[y(t) = \quad \boxed{\phantom{-e^{-5t}}}\]

Page 5

Warm Up — Phase Portrait (Solution Revealed)

Diagram description: A GeoGebra phase portrait is shown for the system \(f(x,y) = 5x\), \(g(x,y) = -5y\), so \(\mathbf{x}' = \begin{bmatrix} 5x \\ -5y \end{bmatrix}\). The vector field shows a saddle pattern: arrows point outward along the horizontal (\(x\)) axis and inward toward the horizontal axis along the vertical direction. Parameters \(C_1 = 1.1\), \(C_2 = 1.1\). The solution curve formulas are displayed: \(x(t) = -4e^{5t}\) and \(y(t) = -e^{-5t}\). Starting at the blue dot \((-4, -1)\), the red trajectory moves rapidly to the left (as \(x\) grows in magnitude in the negative direction) while \(y\) decays toward zero, hugging close to the negative \(x\)-axis.

Particular solution: \(x(t) = -4e^{5t}\), \(\quad y(t) = -e^{-5t}\)

Page 6

Simple IVP 1 — Uncoupled System Overview

Solve for the solution curve \(\vec{r}(t) = \begin{bmatrix} x(t) \\ y(t) \end{bmatrix}\) so that \(\vec{r}(0) = \begin{bmatrix} x_0 \\ y_0 \end{bmatrix}\) and

\[\begin{cases} \dfrac{dx}{dt} = ax \\[8pt] \dfrac{dy}{dt} = by \end{cases} \qquad \text{or equivalently} \qquad \vec{r}\,'(t) = \begin{bmatrix} ax \\ by \end{bmatrix}\]

Solution:

\[\vec{r}(t) = \begin{bmatrix} x_0 e^{at} \\ y_0 e^{bt} \end{bmatrix}\]

Observations:

  • The origin is always an equilibrium.
  • Flow is along the axes.
  • If \(a, b > 0\): source.
  • If \(a, b < 0\): sink.
  • Mixed signs: node/saddle.

Page 7

Simple IVP 2 — Partially Coupled System (Setup)

Solve for the solution curve \(\vec{r}(t) = \begin{bmatrix} x(t) \\ y(t) \end{bmatrix}\) so that \(\vec{r}(0) = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix}\) and

\[\begin{cases} \dfrac{dx}{dt} = 2x + y \\[8pt] \dfrac{dy}{dt} = 2y \end{cases} \qquad \text{or equivalently} \qquad \vec{r}\,'(t) = \begin{bmatrix} 2x + y \\ 2y \end{bmatrix}\]

Observation: We cannot solve the \(\dfrac{dx}{dt}\) equation first (it depends on both \(x\) and \(y\)), but we do know how to solve the \(\dfrac{dy}{dt}\) equation. It is the same as before — separable:

\[y(t) = Ce^{2t}\]

Page 8

Simple IVP 2 — Solving for \(x(t)\) via Integrating Factor

Substitute \(y(t) = Ce^{2t}\) back into the \(\dfrac{dx}{dt}\) equation to get a linear first-order ODE:

  1. \(\dfrac{dx}{dt} = 2x + Ce^{2t}\)
  2. \(\Rightarrow\quad \dfrac{dx}{dt} - 2x = Ce^{2t}\)    (both sides have the same exponential rate)
  3. Integrating factor: \(\mu(t) = e^{\int -2\,dt} = e^{-2t}\)
  4. \(\Rightarrow\quad \dfrac{d}{dt}\!\left[x \cdot e^{-2t}\right] = C\)
  5. Integrate both sides: \(\displaystyle x \cdot e^{-2t} = Ct + D\)
  6. \(\Rightarrow\quad x(t) = (Ct + D)e^{2t}\)

Page 9

Simple IVP 2 — General and Particular Solution

The general solution is:

\[\vec{r}(t) = \begin{bmatrix} x(t) \\ y(t) \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} (Ct + D)e^{2t} \\ Ce^{2t} \end{bmatrix} = C\begin{bmatrix} t \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}e^{2t} + D\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}e^{2t}\]

Applying the initial condition \(\vec{r}(0) = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix}\):

\[\vec{r}(0) = \begin{bmatrix} D \\ C \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix} \qquad \Rightarrow \qquad D = 1,\quad C = 3\]

The particular solution is:

\[\vec{r}(t) = \begin{bmatrix} (3t + 1)e^{2t} \\ 3e^{2t} \end{bmatrix}\]

Page 10

Simple IVP 2 — Phase Portrait

Diagram description: A GeoGebra phase portrait for the system \(f(x,y) = 2x + y\), \(g(x,y) = 2y\), so \(\mathbf{x}' = \begin{bmatrix} 2x+y \\ 2y \end{bmatrix}\). The vector field shows arrows pointing outward from the origin in all directions, consistent with a source. Parameters \(C_1 = 1.1\), \(C_2 = 1.1\). Solution functions displayed: \(x(t) = (3t+1)e^{2t}\), \(y(t) = 3e^{2t}\). Starting at the blue dot \((1, 3)\), the red trajectory curves upward and to the right, rapidly growing away from the origin in the first quadrant, closely following a ray emanating from the origin as both \(x\) and \(y\) grow exponentially.

Page 11

Simple IVP 2 — Activity

Solve for the solution curve \(\vec{r}(t) = \begin{bmatrix} x(t) \\ y(t) \end{bmatrix}\) so that \(\vec{r}(0) = \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}\) and

\[\begin{cases} \dfrac{dx}{dt} = -x + y \\[8pt] \dfrac{dy}{dt} = -y \end{cases} \qquad \text{or equivalently} \qquad \vec{r}\,'(t) = \begin{bmatrix} -x + y \\ -y \end{bmatrix}\]

Students are asked to solve this system using the same method as IVP 2: first solve the separable \(dy/dt\) equation, then substitute into the \(dx/dt\) equation and solve using an integrating factor.

Page 12

Simple IVP 2 — Partially Coupled System Overview

Solve for the solution curve \(\vec{r}(t) = \begin{bmatrix} x(t) \\ y(t) \end{bmatrix}\) so that \(\vec{r}(0) = \begin{bmatrix} x_0 \\ y_0 \end{bmatrix}\) and

\[\begin{cases} \dfrac{dx}{dt} = ax + y \\[8pt] \dfrac{dy}{dt} = ay \end{cases} \qquad \text{or equivalently} \qquad \vec{r}\,'(t) = \begin{bmatrix} ax + y \\ ay \end{bmatrix}\]

General Solution:

\[\vec{r}(t) = \begin{bmatrix} x(t) \\ y(t) \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} (Ct + D)e^{at} \\ Ce^{at} \end{bmatrix}\]

Observations:

  • The origin is an equilibrium.
  • Flow is along the \(x\)-axis.
  • If \(a > 0\): source.
  • If \(a < 0\): sink.

Page 13

Substitution Strategies

The amazing thing is that all first-order linear systems with constant coefficients in 2 variables become one of these types given a good substitution.

So the strategy is:

  • Find good substitutions.
  • Substitute and solve (uncoupled or partially coupled).
  • Substitute back.

Page 14

Complex Numbers — Introduction

Real numbers \(\mathbb{R}\) put a number system on the line.

Diagram description: A number line is sketched with a point marked at 0 and an arrow pointing right labeled \(r\), representing the real number line.

Complex numbers \(\mathbb{C} = \{a + bi \mid a, b \in \mathbb{R}\}\) put a number system on the plane.

Page 15

Complex Numbers — The Imaginary Unit and Addition

\(i\) has the property that \(i^2 = -1\).

Diagram description: A coordinate plane (the complex plane) is sketched. The horizontal axis is the real axis (labeled \(a\)) and the vertical axis is the imaginary axis (labeled \(b\)). A point is plotted at \((a, b)\) and labeled \(a + bi\), showing how a complex number corresponds to a point in the plane.

Addition:

\[(a + bi) + (c + di) = (a + c) + (b + d)i\]
Diagram description: A second sketch illustrates complex addition geometrically. Two vectors from the origin are shown: one to the point \(a + bi\) and one to \(c + di\). Their vector sum points to \((a+c) + (b+d)i\), following the parallelogram law.

Page 16

Complex Numbers — Multiplication

Multiplication: Just FOIL, then use \(i^2 = -1\):

\[(a + bi)(c + di) = ac + bci + adi + bdi^2 = (ac - bd) + (ad + bc)i\]

where \((ac - bd)\) is the real part and \((ad + bc)\) is the imaginary part.

Multiplying by \(i\) is a rotation CCW by \(90^\circ\):

\[(a + bi) \cdot i = -b + ai\]
Diagram description (top right): A small matrix multiplication example is sketched, \(\begin{bmatrix} a \\ b \end{bmatrix} \cdot \begin{bmatrix} -b \\ a \end{bmatrix}\), with the result labeled “0”, illustrating an example of orthogonality or a dot product being zero.

Page 17

Complex Numbers — Notation and Complex Conjugate

It is common to write \(z = x + iy\) where \(x, y \in \mathbb{R}\).

  • The real part of \(z\): \(\operatorname{Re}(z) = x\)
  • The imaginary part of \(z\): \(\operatorname{Im}(z) = y\)
  • The complex conjugate of \(z\): \(\bar{z} = x - iy\)

Observe:

\[\tfrac{1}{2}(z + \bar{z}) = \operatorname{Re}(z) \qquad \tfrac{1}{2i}(z - \bar{z}) = \operatorname{Im}(z)\]

Page 18

Complex Numbers — Euler’s Formula

Euler’s Formula connects Cartesian and polar forms:

\[re^{i\theta} = x + iy\]

where \(r\) is the modulus (distance from origin) and \(\theta\) is the argument (angle from positive real axis). This is derived via Taylor expansion.

Diagram description: A coordinate plane is sketched. A point \(x + iy\) is shown in the first quadrant. A line segment of length \(r\) connects the origin to the point, making an angle \(\theta\) with the positive \(x\)-axis. This illustrates the polar representation \(r e^{i\theta}\).

Page 19

Simple IVP 3 — Complex Uncoupled System (Setup)

Solve for the solution curve \(\vec{r}(t) = \begin{bmatrix} x(t) \\ y(t) \end{bmatrix}\) so that \(\vec{r}(0) = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}\) and

\[\begin{cases} \dfrac{dx}{dt} = x - 2y \\[8pt] \dfrac{dy}{dt} = 2x + y \end{cases} \qquad \text{or equivalently} \qquad \vec{r}\,'(t) = \begin{bmatrix} x - 2y \\ 2x + y \end{bmatrix}\]

With an appropriate substitution, this system becomes uncoupled. Define complex variables:

\[\begin{cases} u = x + iy \\ v = x - iy \end{cases}\]

Then:

\[\frac{du}{dt} = \frac{dx}{dt} + i\frac{dy}{dt}\]

Page 20

Simple IVP 3 — Complex Uncoupled System (Derivation)

Continuing from the substitution \(u = x + iy\), compute \(\dfrac{du}{dt}\):

  1. \(\dfrac{du}{dt} = \dfrac{dx}{dt} + i\,\dfrac{dy}{dt}\)
  2. \(= (x - 2y) + i(2x + y)\)
  3. \(= (1 + 2i)x + (-2 + i)y\)
  4. Since \((-2 + i) = (1 + 2i) \cdot i\) (multiplication by \(i\) rotates by \(90^\circ\)): \[= (1 + 2i)x + (1 + 2i)(iy) = (1 + 2i)(x + iy) = (1 + 2i)u\]

So \(\dfrac{du}{dt} = (1 + 2i)\,u\) — this is an uncoupled separable ODE in \(u\) alone, which can be solved directly as in IVP 1.
